Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy is a point-and-click adventure that answers the question:

> “What if we gave you Sherlock’s brain… but *none* of his patience?”

You’re invited to investigate a mysteriously abandoned mansion museum.
In practice, you will:

* Click on 3 pixels per second
* Solve 19th-century OSHA violations
* Develop a deep hatred of sarcophagi

---

### Pros:

* Peak early-2000s adventure energy: static pre-rendered rooms, weird camera angles, and puzzles designed by someone who’s never heard the phrase “too obscure.”
* Sherlock occasionally says something smug like, “Elementary,” after you solve a puzzle you brute-forced by randomly combining items for 10 minutes.
* Inventory full of extremely specific trash: broken rods, mysterious keys, clock hands, half a cog, some rope, one brick, emotional damage.
* Every room feels like an escape room built by a museum curator who *really* didn’t want visitors.

---

### Cons:

* Difficulty curve:

  * Tutorial: “Turn key, open door.”
  * 10 minutes later: “Align the ancient mechanism using a code hidden in a painting you didn’t realize was interactable.”
* Miss one tiny hotspot and you’ll spend 30 minutes walking in circles like a Victorian Roomba.
* The mummy isn’t even the scariest thing here – it’s the realization you’ve been stuck on the same lock for half an hour.
* Sherlock’s voice lines give “I’m judging you” energy every time you fail at basic observation. And he’s right.

---

### Peak Holmes Experience:

* Examining the same statue five times because *this* click might be the magic one.
* Picking up 12 useless objects and somehow missing the one item that actually matters.
* Solving a ridiculously convoluted mechanism, opening the door, and immediately saving because you know you’re not doing that again.
* Finishing a chapter and confidently saying, “If I lived back then, I could’ve been a detective,” while your browser history is 90% “sherlock mummy walkthrough part 3.”

---

7.5/10
It’s clunky, old, and occasionally unfair, but if you like classic janky puzzle adventures and being told you’re dumber than Sherlock Holmes, it’s beautiful.

Would click on every wall, insult the mummy’s interior design, and pretend I solved the puzzles without a guide again.

I remember when Bionic Commando Rearmed first came out on the PlayStation 3. I bought it right away and absolutely loved the music, the gameplay, and just the overall feel of it. Later, when I switched to PC, I was so excited to see it was available there too. It was the same with the other Bionic Commando game—the one with the dreads. I bought both of them back when they originally released on PS3.

Back then, I remember Rearmed being incredibly difficult, and I never managed to beat it. Coming back to it now reminded me why I liked it so much. The controls feel really tight, and the swinging mechanic is still one of the coolest movement systems in any platformer.

This was actually the first game I played on my ROG Ally X. Ironically, I could never get it working properly on my desktop PC, even after trying a bunch of tutorials online. The handheld had no issues, so I ended up playing the entire game there.

One thing I really like is that this isn’t a Metroidvania. You simply pick a level, beat it, and move on. Every stage feels like its own platforming puzzle, and the bosses are puzzles too. It’s not just about having fast reflexes—you have to figure out each boss’s mechanics before you can beat them, which makes every fight feel rewarding.

There are around 19 levels. Some are full stages while others are shorter transition areas, but I actually like that structure because I can jump into a level, focus on beating it, and call it a day instead of wandering through one giant interconnected map. Defeating bosses also rewards you with new weapons and upgrades, like bazookas, pistol upgrades, machine guns, and character enhancements, so it always feels like you’re making progress.

Now for the part where I have a love-hate relationship with the game: that final level. It honestly felt as long as, if not longer than, all the previous stages. It reminded me of the old Gauntlet games where you have a limited number of lives and just keep inching a little farther every attempt. I had to memorize every section. The Albatross stage in particular really was the albatross around my neck—I genuinely thought I wasn’t going to beat the game because of it.

Even after getting through all those sections, you only have so many lives left for the final boss. Eventually I got consistent enough to reach the boss with five lives almost every run, but then I had to learn the boss itself, which is also extremely difficult. The frustrating part is that it takes so long to get back to the fight that practicing the boss is a challenge in itself.

When I finally beat it, though, it felt amazing. It wasn’t one of those “I’m just glad it’s over and never want to play it again” moments. It was the kind of victory that feels earned. I’m pretty sure if I went back now I’d beat that final level much faster because it’s one of those games where persistence and learning the patterns eventually pays off.

I also played the game on the hardest difficulty available for a brand-new save file. I know there’s an even harder difficulty that unlocks afterward, but this was the toughest setting you can choose from the start, and it felt like the perfect challenge.

Overall, I loved Bionic Commando Rearmed. The soundtrack is fantastic, the controls are incredibly tight, the swinging mechanic is still one of the most satisfying movement systems around, and I really enjoyed the level-by-level structure instead of another Metroidvania. It’s a challenging game, but one that always feels fair once you learn it.

It’s also a shame that Bionic Commando Rearmed 2 isn’t available on Steam. I’ve heard it’s not nearly as good, but I’d still like the chance to play it because this game reminded me why I liked the series so much in the first place.

It’s alright, not as jagged or weird as quake 1 which makes it way less interesting as a piece of video game history imo. A lot of people say that the visuals in this game are really bland and I have to agree. Lots of browns and greys. Not that quake 1 was bursting with saturated colors or anything, but the gothic and medieval horror vibe of quake 1 was more interesting from a tonal perspective than the straightforward sci-fi feel of this game. That first game was so inscrutable and moody and it felt like the dark color palette was a big part of that. A sci-fi setting could’ve benefited from a little bit more color and detail, but it feels like they just did the visuals of quake 1 again without understanding why the dingy aesthetic of that game fit so well. 

It’s worth noting that Trent Reznor, who refused to come back to the series to do the ost for quake 2 as he did for the original, voiced a lot of these criticisms too. He said quake 2 had no atmosphere. I don’t know if I fully agree with that, but put up against the first game it’s easy to see where he’s coming from. Maybe he didn’t feel like the game was sufficiently dissonant enough for his tastes. Quake 1’s single player is nothing if not atonal and weird. It’s a game with hastily thrown together elements from completely contrasting vibes, level designers who couldn’t agree on anything, and with almost no attempt to make it cohere at all. It is something that you would never see today. No serious or experienced game designer in 2026 would even think to make something like Quake 1. Quake 2, unlike basically any other game, suffers by sticking to a more coherent vision.

Abe's Oddysee is still a classic, but running it on a modern PC takes a bit of setup. Out of the box, my CPU fans blew like crazy and hit 75C because the 1997 engine runs an uncapped single-core loop that pushes one CPU core at full boost voltage, even on the main menu.

I spent a long time testing standard fixes like setting a global or program specific max frame rate in GPU software, or changing CPU affinity in Task Manager and researched other solutions but didn't bother trying riskier things with the registry, BIOS and so on. None of what I tried worked because they don't stop the internal code loop from maxing out that single core.

Here is what actually fixed everything for me:

1. Finding & Adding the Executable
Auto-scans in GPU software won't detect this game. You have to manually add AbeWin.exe to your NVIDIA graphics program settings as well as Windows Graphics Settings to force your dedicated GPU (if you have a CPU with integrated graphics) and apply other custom profile options. (However frame limiters won't work like I said earlier.)

2. Visual & Scaling Fixes
Right-click AbeWin.exe > Properties > Compatibility tab:

Check Disable fullscreen optimizations.

Click Change high DPI settings, check Override high DPI scaling behavior, and set it to Application.

In your GPU control panel or App, make sure the scaling device is your GPU, Override the Scaling Mode Set by Games and Programs is checked and lastly enable GPU Integer Scaling as the mode. On a 1440p monitor, this gives you a sharp 1920x1440 centered picture with clean black sidebars instead of a blurry stretched image that aspect ratio gives. For other resolutions, you'll have to research that because integer scaling needs to divide evenly to work best, but on a 2560x1440p display panel the math works out for integer scaling with this game; you can switch back to Aspect Ratio whenever for other games. 

3. Fixing the CPU Heat & Fan Noise
Go to Windows Control Panel > Hardware and Sound > Power Options > Create a Power Plan (left side of the window) > create a custom plan name at the bottom (I named mine "Old Games")  and save it with default options > Change Plan Settings > Change Advanced Power Settings > Processor Power Management > set Maximum Processor State to 95%. This turns off CPU Turbo Boost voltage spikes for any programs while the plan is on, dropping my CPU temps from 75C down to a completely silent 41C with zero performance loss. I made a desktop shortcut for Power Options to swap to this plan when playing old unoptimized games like this that lack normal support. 

Once those quick steps are done, the game runs quiet and cool and when you aren't playing this game you just switch back to your recommended or default profile you normally use.

This is my first review on Steam.  
First: cap the frames to 60 (or 45 for Deck) to avoid physics bugs.  I played vanilla on Deck with no issues.  As of writing this review I am 80%+ through the main story (about 4 missions left) and have done quite a bit of side content.

I have completed all major Far Cry games on console (multiple times), but this is the best.  It is very disturbingly existential in its gameplay systems.  The factions give you pointless and amoral missions that serve only to perpetuate the conflict.  The routine nature of having to fix your vehicles, clear checkpoints,  and murder people to get to your objective.  The constant need to replace weapons and obtain malaria meds due to weapon and bodily degradation.  People say the respawning checkpoints are annoying, but without them the world would be empty and devoid of challenge.  Further, the checkpoints add to the feeling of futility and that you don't meaningfully impact the state of the country.  There is very little narrative; most of the game's expression of futile, routine, and amoral murder and chaos is expressed through its gameplay systems.  Most Far Cry games are morally ambiguous, but there is no ambiguity here, just pure amorality.  However, this is not going to be to everyone's taste.  Some people will find it frustrating and boring, I guess.  I loved it.  It does mess with your head a bit, though as it is a much bleaker game than the ones that came after.

Finally, the visuals are beautiful.  The character models are a bit dated, but passable, and the environment and atmosphere are top notch.

I honestly didn't expect to get this invested in EVE Online. I downloaded it out of curiosity, thinking it would be another space MMO where you pick a ship, complete some missions, fight enemies and slowly upgrade your equipment. Well, I couldn't have been more wrong.

The first thing that stands out is just how much freedom this game gives you. There isn't really one correct way to play. You can become a miner, explorer, trader, industrialist, pirate or focus entirely on combat. You can spend hours building your economy, transporting goods between systems, searching for hidden locations or joining other players in large-scale fleet operations. And somehow, all these activities are connected to each other.

The player-driven economy is probably one of my favourite aspects. Almost everything has a purpose, and the market feels like an actual ecosystem rather than a shop with items randomly generated by developers. Players produce ships, gather resources, manufacture equipment and transport goods across the galaxy. Even something as simple as buying a new ship can involve a surprisingly complicated chain of player activities behind the scenes.

I also really like the atmosphere. Flying through different star systems, looking at distant planets, stations and massive ships gives you a strange feeling of being part of something much bigger than your own character. Sometimes I just find myself travelling somewhere with music playing in the background, checking the map and planning my next destination. It sounds boring on paper, but there is something relaxing about it.

Of course, EVE isn't perfect. The learning curve is absolutely brutal for newcomers. There are so many menus, statistics, mechanics and things to understand that it can feel like starting a new job rather than playing a game. The tutorials help, but they only introduce a fraction of what is actually available. You will probably spend quite a bit of time looking things up, watching guides and asking more experienced players for advice.

Another thing worth mentioning is that the game doesn't always respect your expectations. You can spend hours collecting resources or preparing for an expedition and lose everything because of one bad decision or an encounter with another player. Ships are not simply temporary equipment that magically returns after destruction. Losing something expensive genuinely hurts, especially when you know how much time it took to afford it. But strangely enough, that's also what makes the victories feel meaningful.

The community is another interesting part of the experience. You can meet incredibly helpful people willing to explain complicated mechanics, share knowledge and even help you get started. At the same time, there are plenty of players who will happily take advantage of your lack of experience. Trusting the wrong person can become an expensive lesson. I guess that's part of the charm of a universe where other players are not just background characters.

I wouldn't recommend rushing through everything or trying to understand the entire game immediately. There is simply too much content, and constantly comparing your progress to experienced players is probably the fastest way to burn yourself out. Find an activity you enjoy, learn it properly and expand from there. Joining a decent corporation can also completely change your experience.

Despite its age, EVE Online still offers something that is surprisingly difficult to find in modern MMOs: a world where players create their own stories and where decisions can have consequences beyond a simple quest reward.

It's complicated, sometimes frustrating, occasionally incredibly slow, and definitely not for everyone. But if you enjoy space exploration, strategy, economics, social interaction and the freedom to create your own goals, there is a good chance you'll find something special here.

I still have a ridiculous amount of things to learn and explore, and that's probably the best reason to keep playing.

I'll have to be honest about this. The game itself is fun to play, but Egosoft needs their knuckles rapped for the pathetic story line (if you can even call it that).  One should expect to see continuity between XBTF and X:Tension, but X:tension simply doesn't provide it.  Hey, remember me? I'm  Kyle Brennan, the Hero of Argon and loved by all of the races for my part in the Xenon War. So then why does no one even know me now, plus the Split and Piranad are downright hostile? I was in a sector called Brennan's Triumph, and the Split told me to sod off. What happened to my trading empire and my million plus credits I usually carried with me?  Egosoft no doubt spent quite a bit of money developing that video with the kid telling us about Captain Brennan. Unfortunately, the video does nothing to explain what happened to Brennan's mines and fabs, or why the prices of almost everything have skyrocketed. Would it have been so hard to find a reason?  Of course not. I took a few minutes and came up with this:   After the Xenon's mother ship was destroyed, Ban Danna gave Brennan those fantastic 125mw shields, which he promptly used to wipe out the Xenon ships and bases in all of their sectors. In retaliation, the Xenon staged a major attack that destroyed all of Brennan's possessions and caused prices to skyrocket among all of the races. The Xenon also put a large bounty on Brennan's life, causing Ban Danna to advise him to go incognito for a while. Danna gave him an Argon buster and a few thousand credits to start out on his own. (Brennan couldn't draw on his own account, since that would reveal where he was.)  And then the game could proceed as it does, but at least there would be a reason for Brennan's sudden poverty and unpopularity. Surely their professional writers could have done even better. Having said that, I do like the way the game is put together and recommend it for many hours of fun.  Still, Egosoft really dropped the ball when it came to setting the stage for Brennan's new adventures.
